lesson.content:
## What it is
Routing algorithms are decision-making processes used by routers to determine the best path for a packet to travel from its source to its destination. [p. 1]
## Real-life analogy
Imagine a postal service where each post office (router) keeps a map of the best routes to all other post offices (routers). When a letter (packet) arrives at a post office, it uses this map to decide which post office to send the letter to next. [p. 1]
## How it works
1. **Each router maintains a routing table**: This table contains information about the best path to reach other routers. [p. 1]
2. **Routers use the optimality principle**: If a path is the best way to reach one router, it will also be the best way to reach another router that is on that path. [p. 1]
## Key terms
- **Optimality principle**: If router J is on the optimal path from I to K, then the optimal path from J to K follows the same route. [p. 1]
## Example
Consider a network with four routers: A, B, C, and D. The routing table for router A might look like this: [p. 1]
- **Destination**: B, **Distance**: 2, **Next Hop**: B [p. 2]
- **Destination**: C, **Distance**: 1, **Next Hop**: C [p. 2]
- **Destination**: D, **Distance**: 7, **Next Hop**: B [p. 2]

Router A learns from router B that router B reaches router D in 5. Therefore, router A reaches router D in 2 + 5 = 7 through router B, which beats 1 + 7 = 8 through router C. [p. 1]
## What to draw in the exam
No diagram needed. [p. 1]
## Exam tip
Examiners often ask about the optimality principle and how it applies to routing decisions. Make sure to understand how paths are chosen based on the optimality principle. [p. 1]
